OpenWorm

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
... scientists in the US have copied a biological brain and uploaded it into a computer and it worked.

Unique Selling Point:
Cutting edge new technology with massive implications for humanity

Summary:
The brain is really little more than a collection of electrical signals. If we can learn to catalogue those then, in theory, you could upload someone's mind into a computer, allowing them to live forever as a digital form of consciousness. But it's not just science fiction. Sure, scientists aren't anywhere near close to achieving such a feat with humans (and even if they could, the ethics would be pretty fraught), but there's few better examples than the time an international team of researchers managed to do just that with the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans.

Further information:
Scientists Put a Worm Brain in a Lego Robot Body - And It Worked

The brainwaves of a roundworm drove a Lego robot.

The brain is really little more than a collection of electrical signals. If we can learn to catalogue those then, in theory, you could upload someone's mind into a computer, allowing them to live forever as a digital form of consciousness, just like in the Johnny Depp film Transcendence.

But it's not just science fiction. Sure, scientists aren't anywhere near close to achieving such a feat with humans (and even if they could, the ethics would be pretty fraught), but there's few better examples than the time an international team of researchers managed to do just that with the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans.

C. elegans is a little nematodes that have been extensively studied by scientists - we know all their genes and their nervous system has been analysed many times.

So, in 2014, a collective called the OpenWorm project mapped all the connections between the worm's 302 neurons and managed to simulate them in software, as Marissa Fessenden reports for the Smithsonian.

The ultimate goal of the project was to completely replicate C. elegans as a virtual organism. But as an amazing starting point, they managed to simulate its brain, and then they uploaded that into a simple Lego robot.

This Lego robot has all the equivalent limited body parts that C. elegans has - a sonar sensor that acts as a nose, and motors that replace the worm's motor neurons on each side of its body.

Amazingly, without any instruction being programmed into the robot, the C. elegans virtual brain controlled and moved the Lego robot.

Lucy Black wrote for I Programmer:

"It is claimed that the robot behaved in ways that are similar to observed C. elegans. Stimulation of the nose stopped forward motion. Touching the anterior and posterior touch sensors made the robot move forward and back accordingly. Stimulating the food sensor made the robot move forward."

This video of the Lego-worm-robot was released by Timothy Busbice, a founder of OpenWorm, showing it moving, stopping and then travelling backwards.

Of course, the brain simulation still isn't exact. For one, the researchers had to simplify the process that triggers an artificial neuron to fire. But the fact that this robot can move, can stop before it bumps into something and reverse using nothing more than a network of connections that mimic a worm's brain, is pretty incredible.

The OpenWorm project continues to this day, extending itself to make simulations and visualisations available through your web browser.

Scientists are now working out how to map all the connections in the human brain - something called the connectome. Even if we're not uploading our brains into computers, just being able to simulate a human brain would help to revolutionize artificial intelligence and computers.

And if we could one day get to the point where we can somehow get our minds to escape the vulnerable fleshy meat sacks that currently house them, the opportunities would, quite literally, be mind-blowing.

To make the insert local we will also interview Bronwyn Williams an expert in Transhumanism.

Script:


V/O:
Ever since the dawn of humanity people have thought of extending their existence on this earth beyond what nature has given them. They dreamt of living forever… However, this has always been an unattainable ambition, but not anymore.
LINK:
A few pieces of Lego blocks and the brain of a small worm have now put the dream of living forever well and truly within humanity’s grasp.
V/O:
And this new era in human existence has been heralded by this little Lego robot.

Living forever is part of the objective of a branch of science called Transhumanism.
Bronwyn:
Transhumanism is trying to look at how we can exceed our natural capabilities, our natural life span, our natural intellect and our natural health beyond that what nature has given just as is. So, if you are in an accident and you lose your hand you could replace it with a bionic limb. If you have any disease you will be able to cure it, and that included even diseases such as ageing which is basically a disease; it should be curable according to people that are exploring this space.
V/O:
Bronwyn Williams is a futurist and trends analyst. She says trans humanism’s ultimate aim is living forever. It is also called a-mortality.
Bronwyn:
A-mortality is like immortality but you could still die if you are involved in an accident but if you have achieved a-mortality you basically would have cured all diseases, including old age.
V/O:
And this goes hand in hand with the idea of combining humans with technology to fix damage, make them longer lasting and stronger, and thus more than human – transhuman.
LINK
There is actually a term for this merging of technology and humans – we call them cyborgs.
Bronwyn:
Cyborgs is basically any connection between technology and the human body. It is adifferent way we can look at achieving transhumanism or a-mortality. So anything from a contact lens would be considered a cyborg modification, or a pacemaker or an audio implant.
V/O:
Raymond McCauley, a Digital Biology specialist in Silicon Valley, says that nearly all modern humans are actually cyborgs.
Ray:
The idea that we can upgrade ourselves, you know, anything from prosthetic to being an advanced cyborg. People do not realise that this is something that is already set very firmly in civilization. So you will very rarely meet a person who is not a cyborg. Anybody who has ever had a vaccination, well they are not just a natural human being, they have a[product of an advance civilization that has programmed and reformatted their immune system. So, if you ever got a vaccination shot, you are a cyborg.
V/O:
And new technologies allow for many more far reaching modifications of human beings
• we can modify our genes to eliminate diseases
• it is possible to modify embryos to create designer babies
• we can control robotic arms with our thoughts

However, the ultimate in Transhumanism remains the quest for a-mortality, of indefinitely exceeding the normal human life span. A few years ago, a group of scientists decided to achieve this by looking at the brain. They asked the following:
Ray:
What if we could just go ahead and copy a mind. If we could use our technology to look at every neuron in the human brain and see where it is and what it is connected to and then go and make a copy of that but then not run it on you meat hardware run it on digital hardware.
V/O:
This would mean that the brain could continue to exist indefinitely and independent of a body. It would be achieving a-mortality. However, our current technology is not advanced far enough to do this with the 100 billion neurons, and 10 trillion neural connections of the human brain.
LINK:
So, the scientists turned to a more manageable creature to start their quest to achieve a-mortality – a tiny worm.
V/O:
The scientists decided to focus their attention on Caenorhabditis Elegans or C Eelgans for short. It is about 1mm in length and one of the most studied creatures on earth.

They also threw the research open to anybody anywhere in the world and called the project OpenWorm.

C Elegans is a simple organism – it only has about 1000 cells and only three hundred and two neurons that control the worm’s thought processes and movements.
Ray:
And it lives in a very uncomplicated environment. It basically swims around in goo. It is like a basic compilation of all the greatest hits of organisms, it is looking for food, it trying to get away from danger and it is also seeking members of the opposite sex, which I know a lot of people who are exactly like that.
V/O:
The worm’s brain functions and its nervous system have been mapped in the past, so the Open Worm researchers had a good idea of the patterns in which neurons fired for a specific activity -- be it smell, or movement or detecting obstacles.

They then managed to replicate these firing patterns of the neurons in a digital format that mimicked an actual natural worm. This is a simulated worm brain controlling a digital worm in a digital environment.
LINK:
The digital brain worked well in the digital world. The next question was: would it work in the real world?
Ray:
The amazing thing is that once you got this neural network created electronically as bits of code, that code, because of the way we deal with our code now, you can run that on a super computer, you can run it on a small computer, you can run it on a cell phone, you can actually put that in a piece of hardware in the real world and put it into a robot. And one of the people who works with OpenWorm Foundation took the code and put it into a little Lego robot and used the real world environment to simulate the environment. The longitudinal muscles that would make the worm move they hooked to the motors of two wheels, the senses the worm had they hooked to a sound sensor so it would treat different sounds as food and then go and seek those out. And it is amazing you can see the robot boots up and starts running the code and it starts moving around through the world a lot like one of these worms does. It is a worm’s brain controlling a robot.
V/O:
Since this first robot, several other scientists have also put the worm brain code in all kinds of hardware and it continues to turn moving models into food-searching worms.

And this is just the beginning. It will one day be possible to put a human brain on a microchip in the same way.
Bronwyn:
It is another form of transhumanism. In theory you could live forever if your brain was uniquely mapped with your unique neural patterns and implanted in the cloud that artificial intelligence could live on even after natural body had died.
V/O:
But apart from achieving a-mortality, duplicating a human brain on a microchip raises all kinds of new conundrums.
Ray:
If you could duplicate the brain could you duplicate both the consciousness, the neural processing, the way you act and react, things you have learned including all of your memories, you know. How did your birthday cake taste when you were five years old and what did it feel like when you had your first kiss. What if going to University became a matter of sitting in a comfortable chair and plugging in for an hour and half while we create memories of an entire professional career?
LINK:
What makes the Open Worm Project particularly interesting is that South Africans can also participate because of the way the project is set up.
Bronwyn:
So, the Open Worm project is Open source, you can go onto the website, you can take a look, play around with the software and you can even start to develop your own neural interface if you want to. And I would encourage everyone to start looking at that and getting involved with biohacking their own bodies before someone else does it for you.

The OpenWorm project continues to this day, extending itself to make simulations and visualisations available through your web browser. Scientists are now working out how to map all the connections in the human brain - something called the connectome. Even if we're not uploading our brains into computers, just being able to simulate a human brain would help to revolutionize artificial intelligence and computers. And if we could one day get to the point where we can somehow get our minds to escape the vulnerable fleshy meat sacks that currently house them, the opportunities would, quite literally, be mind-blowing. To make the insert local we will also interview Bronwyn Williams an expert in Transhumanism.
